catalog_quote: 2.4 Stress. The Dyabugay stress pattern is not quite as intricate as that of Yidiɲ with regard to the interaction of stress and long vowels, however, some interesting observations can be made. (Furthermore there are a few irregularities for which I have no explanations as yet, such as buwál-bugá-ŋ 'speak, talk' which should be búwal-búgay according to the rules set up below). The basic stress pattern is as follows: (i) Stress on long vowels in final closed syllable of a disyllabic word or in second syllable of a trisyllabic word: gulá:y 'these' / guḏá:y 'those' ... wuɽú:ri-l 'to take out' ḏína: 'foot' diná:la LOC/INST' míɲa 'vegetable food' miɲá:la LOC (ii) Stress on first syllable in 2- and 3- syllabic words, with no long vowel in a closed syllable, e.g.: bína 'ear' máɽa 'hand' ḏína: 'foot' wúɽu: 'river' dámari (mythical being) búluru (mythical being) (iii) Stress on first and penultim…

(2) Deciding source is a 1978 ANU honours-thesis sketch grammar whose author calls the stress analysis preliminary; the best available description is her 1991 Handbook of Australian Languages vol. 4 grammar (pp. 245-348), which we do not hold and which is print-only (OUP).
